facts.claim: "Clear The Air" is the closing track of Off With Their Heads' 2010 Epitaph album In Desolation, which came out on a Tuesday, June 8, 2010.
In Desolation was produced by Jacques Wait together with the band. Wait also recorded and engineered it, and the songs are credited to Off With Their Heads.
The album was recorded and engineered in January 2010 at the Terrarium in Minneapolis, MN, and mastered at Sterling Sound. The publisher is I Hate Francis (ASCAP), and Ryan is credited with lyrics.
The band members credited on In Desolation are Justin, Nate, Robbie, Ryan and Zack.
Songs for In Desolation were first recorded for a split EP with Dillinger Four that never came out. After signing to Epitaph, the band finished recording with the same producer, Jacques Wait.
The Star Tribune called "Clear the Air" the album's epic closer.
The A.V. Club quoted the closing track's lyrics about the mask worn to hide what's inside, in a review that called the album's production too slick for the band's emotional style.

Ryan Young said the lyrics of the In Desolation version of "Clear The Air" were very cut and paste. For the 2016 acoustic re-recording, they decided against punching in, so his gasping for air can be heard.

An acoustic version of "Clear The Air" opens the 2016 album Won't Be Missed, released October 25, 2016 on Ryan Young's Anxious and Angry. Young recorded it in Minneapolis with Dan Jensen, John and Joe.

Off With Their Heads is a punk rock band formed in 2002 in Minneapolis. It has had a rotating line-up, and Ryan Young is the singer and guitarist. A music video for "Clear the Air" is listed for 2011.

research.lineage: Off With Their Heads sit in the Minneapolis-born, Fest-circuit gritty punk and melodic hardcore tradition, and their Epitaph debut was likened to bands such as The Bronx and Against Me!.

draft:
Near the end of **Clear The Air**, Ryan Young stops explaining and starts bargaining. "Don't leave yet," he sings, promising he hasn't reached the part that makes sense of everything. He never does reach it. The song circles back to its opening, the lines about wanting to tell, wanting to share, the fear that "I'll choke to death if I don't clear the air," and tacks "right now" onto the end. The whole confession turns out to be the run-up to one that still hasn't been said.

That's the feeling Off With Their Heads chose to close In Desolation, their 2010 Epitaph album, with: the panic of saying the hard thing out loud to someone who sleeps beside you. Young admits that the face this person sees from morning to night "is the mask that I put on to hide what's inside," and that it stays on until they fall asleep. The shame comes with real tenderness. He tells them it isn't their fault when he begs and pleads. He worries they'll get scared because they have no frame of reference. Then he asks them to stay anyway and catch him before he falls. He wants to protect them from what's inside him, and he wants them to hold it. The song never picks one.

The bluntest lines are the plainest. He calls himself a failure who will never be significant. He thought getting older would make it go away, and instead it got worse. He says being alone is getting harder, and that's why he has to tell them. There's no metaphor to hide behind except the mask, and he's taking that off.

The band doesn't soften any of it. Distorted guitars drive a palm-muted riff at a fast clip, the bass holds to root notes, and the snare hits hard. Young's voice is raw and hoarse, more a melodic shout than singing, with no harmonies to share the load. That's the Minneapolis punk the band has played since 2002, the gritty Fest-circuit strain that got this Epitaph debut compared to The Bronx and Against Me!. The confession isn't whispered at a kitchen table. It's hollered over a full band.

The Star Tribune called it the album's epic closer. Jacques Wait produced it with the band at the Terrarium in Minneapolis, and some of these songs were first cut for a split with Dillinger Four that never came out. The A.V. Club quoted the mask lines but found the record's production too slick for that kind of feeling. Young seems to have heard something similar. He later called the album version very cut and paste, and when he re-recorded it acoustic to open 2016's Won't Be Missed, they skipped the punch-ins so you can hear him gasping for air.

It sticks because it puts you in the room with someone halfway through the hardest thing they've ever said, pleading with you to stay for an ending they don't have yet.
